title: Use of fentanyl test strips by people who inject drugs: Longitudinal findings from the south atlantic fentanyl test strip study (SAFTSS)

claims.statement: In people who inject drugs attending two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia (recruited June 2021 to March 2022), recent use of fentanyl test strips was less common a year after the start than at the start, and not clearly different after six months: the adjusted odds of having used strips in the past 30 days were 0.642 times those at the start at 12 months (95% CI 0.447 to 0.923; all 541 people) and 0.557 times (0.364 to 0.853) in the 212 who answered all three surveys, and 0.936 times (0.696 to 1.258) at 6 months, while the share of those 212 who had ever used strips rose from 65 to 80 in 100. The share using strips at each survey is not printed, so the size of the fall cannot be given as a number out of 100. 213 of the 541 gave no follow-up and had used strips less often, which could bias the trend, and why use fell was not measured (the authors suggest that a test for fentanyl alone tells people less once fentanyl is expected). Over a few weeks, young adults in a Rhode Island pilot used a median of 3 of the 10 strips they were given (10 of 81 used all ten); in that pilot and in a British Columbia take-home programme, 95 or 96 in 100 said they would use strips again, an intention rather than a measure of use. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Past-30-day use, adjusted odds ratios against baseline (mixed-effects logistic regression): 12 months 0.642 (0.447–0.923; 541 people, 1081 observations) and 0.557 (0.364–0.853; 212 complete cases, 636 observations); 6 months 0.936 (0.696–1.258) and 0.946 (0.650–1.375). Lifetime use among complete cases 65.1% at baseline, 77.8% at 6 months and 79.7% at 12 months. No follow-up: 213 of 541 (39.4%, editors' calculation), who had less often used strips (54.3% against 65.1%). Krieger: median 3 strips (IQR 1–6) within a few weeks; 10 of 81 used all ten; 77/81 (95%) would like to use strips in future. Klaire: 322/336 answers (95.8%) would use strips again.

claims.statement: In people who use drugs in the United States, mostly recruited at harm-reduction services, and in European drug checking studies relayed by one review, people who use test strips or drug checking, compared with people in the same samples who do not, are associated with more fentanyl and heroin use, more injecting, more often having seen an overdose and, in the largest study, already doing more to lower their risk, so simple comparisons of the two groups mix any effect of testing with who chooses to test. At US harm-reduction sites that hand out strips (2023), 414 people who had used strips in the past 30 days and 318 who had not differed in fentanyl use (78 against 59 in 100), injecting (75 against 57 in 100) and ever having been shown how to use strips (76 against 41 in 100); the strip group already reported more of the eight risk-reduction behaviours studied at the start, and its overdose rate was twice as high before allowing for these differences and not clearly different after (risk ratio 2.06, then 1.20). In rural people who inject drugs (2021 to 2023), strip use went with having seen an overdose in the past 6 months (adjusted odds ratio 2.444, 95% CI 1.784 to 3.347), heroin use (1.615, 1.107 to 2.357) and being married or living as married (1.521, 1.084 to 2.134), and less with being unhoused (0.679, 0.504 to 0.913), but not clearly with having overdosed oneself (0.981, 0.676 to 1.424) or with fentanyl use (1.332, 0.948 to 1.872). In a small Rhode Island pilot, the 62 who used a strip differed clearly from the 19 who did not only in more often having sold drugs (84 against 58 in 100), while among those who used a strip, those whose strip showed fentanyl used heroin weekly far more often (20 of 31 against 3 of 31). In three European studies relayed by a review, clients of drug checking services used ecstasy more often than people at the same events who did not use the services. All characteristics were self-reported, and the two larger studies recruited people at harm-reduction services. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Vickers-Smith (strip group against no strip): past 30-day fentanyl use 78.2% against 59.2%, injection 75.1% against 56.6%, ever received strip instructions 76.2% against 40.6% (each P < .001), past 30-day overdose 26.0% against 20.5% (P = .10); nonfatal overdose RR 2.06 (1.09–3.89) unadjusted, 1.20 (0.70–2.06) adjusted. Erickson (adjusted odds ratios, full sample): witnessed overdose 2.444 (1.784–3.347), heroin use 1.615 (1.107–2.357), married 1.521 (1.084–2.134), unhoused 0.679 (0.504–0.913), own overdose 0.981 (0.676–1.424), fentanyl use 1.332 (0.948–1.872). Krieger: ever dealt drugs 52/62 (84%) against 11/19 (58%), p = .038; ever injected 29/62 (47%) against 13/19 (68%), p = .099; positive against no positive result: weekly heroin 20/31 (65%) against 3/31 (10%), ever injected 25/31 (81%) against 8/31 (26%), witnessed overdose 29/31 (94%) against 9/31 (29%).
